idiom_name: iterator/generator protocol plus context managers (with); e.g. zipfile.ZipFile.open and streamed response reads
implementation_notes: Python's local idiom replaces the classic stage plan with two protocols: iterators and generators pull one part at a time, so the consumer's next() is what advances the acquisition, and context managers release the stages that were actually acquired in reverse order on every exit path. The standard library is full of resources that stage themselves: opening a ZipFile reads the central directory and defers each member's decompression until ZipFile.open returns a ZipExtFile whose read, readline and seek operate on that member, and urllib.request.urlopen returns a response object whose headers and status are available before the body is read with read(n). An explicit stage plan is still justified when the resource must be shared between threads or requests (generators are single-consumer) or when parts must be fetched in a different order than the provider lays them out.
code_sketch:
with zipfile.ZipFile("bundle.zip") as zf:       # stage 1: central directory only
    meta = json.loads(zf.read("manifest.json"))  # cheap part, always needed
    with zf.open("payload.bin") as part:         # stage 2: decompress on demand
        for chunk in iter(lambda: part.read(1 << 16), b""):
            sink.write(chunk)                     # bounded, proportional to use
pitfalls: A generator has exactly one consumer: a second traversal needs a re-open or itertools.tee, and an abandoned generator releases its stages only when it is closed or collected, so partially consumed resources need an explicit generator.close().

read() without a size argument is a full acquisition inside the deferred stage; the partiality lives entirely in the size argument, and wrapping a member stream in a text reader can buffer far more than intended.

Closing the outer resource invalidates the inner stage: reading from a member stream after its ZipFile is closed raises, and the same applies to a response whose connection was dropped between stages.
Iterators are single-pass and lazily bound, so wrapping the staged source in list() or a comprehension converts it into a full acquisition without any visible symptom.
functools.partial is partial application, not partial acquisition - searching the standard library by name finds the wrong concept entirely.
